newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban say Afghan opposition loses more ground in north.
newsitem.headline: Taleban say Afghan opposition loses more ground in north.

text.p: The Islamic Taleban said they had seized a strategic pass in central Afghanistan on Tuesday and northern opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum had lost two more cities to pro-Taleban mutineers within his forces.

Maulvi Wakil Ahmad, a senior Taleban official based in the southern city of Kandahar, told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) that forces led by a disaffected Dostum commander, General Abdul Malik, had captured Kunduz, capital of Kunduz province, and Sar-i-Pul, capital of Jowzjan province.
There was no independent confirmation of the latest reported advances by Malik's troops, who launched a Taleban-backed rebellion against Dostum in four northern provinces on Monday.

Malik, governor of Faryab province, declared support for the Taleban on Monday and said he had captured 5,000 Dostum soldiers and two provinces, including Faryab, to the west of Dostum's northern stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif.
Taleban radio said in a broadcast from Kabul on Monday night that the Islamic militia was advancing on Faryab after breaking through Dostum's defences. It gave no details.
But an opposition spokesman said on Tuesday that Taleban forces had not yet entered Faryab and negotiations were continuing to keep Malik in the opposition alliance.

"So far the Taleban have not entered Faryab. We are trying to solve the problem between Malik and Dostum. We have already started this," opposition spokesman Dr Abdullah (one name) told Reuters by telephone from the north.
AIP said on Monday Dostum seemed to have kept control of his stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif, 300 km (187 miles) northwest of Kabul, but there has been no word on his whereabouts.
A Taleban military official in Kabul said Taleban forces had captured the Shibar Pass on Tuesday from an opposition Shi'ite Moslem militia and were advancing towards the town of Bamiyan.
"The Shibar Pass has fallen to our forces and they are advancing towards Bamiyan," the official said.
The fundamentalist Islamic Taleban already had control of two-thirds of the country prior to the latest fighting.

Taleban forces have been facing opposition fighters in the Shibar Pass for more than three months. The pass leads into the Bamiyan valley, stronghold of the mainly Shi'ite Hezb-i-Wahadat faction, one of three main parties in the opposition alliance.
However, a Hezb-i-Wahadat spokesman in Mazar-i-Sharif denied the fall of the pass, saying a Taleban attack had been repulsed.

"The reports of the fall of the Shibar Pass and the advance towards Bamiyan are false propaganda. They launched an attack this morning on the Shibber which was foiled," said Abdul Wahid, Hezb-i-Wahadat's political representative in Mazar-i-Sharif.
There was no independent information on the situation at the battle front.
Aid workers in Mazar-i-Sharif said the road leading south from the town towards the Salang Pass and Kabul was blocked.
"Passengers trying to travel south were all blocked in Khulm, 120 km (76 miles) from Mazar-i-Sharif, by a pro-Malik commander and the road is still blocked," one aid worker said.
